message.content:
### Your Rights as a Tenant in Texas (as of 2026) | Area | What You’re Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |------|------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • The landlord may charge up to **one month’s rent** for a furnished unit and **two months’ rent** for an unfurnished unit.
• The deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a written move‑in inspection report.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions if the landlord withholds any portion. | | **Habitability** | • The landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control). | • Provide written notice of needed repairs.
• If the landlord fails to act, you may file a complaint with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA) or pursue a **repair‑and‑deduct** claim in small‑claims court. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease; late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable. | • Keep records of all payments (bank statements, receipts). | | **Entry Rights** | • Landlord must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hrs) before entering, except in emergencies. | • Document any unnotified entries; you can withhold rent or seek damages if the entry violates the lease or law. | | **Privacy** | • You have the right to privacy in your rented space; the landlord cannot harass or threaten you. | • Report harassment to local law enforcement or the Texas Attorney General’s office. | | **Discrimination** | • Texas law (and federal Fair Housing Act) prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | • File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR) or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party may terminate a month‑to‑month lease with **30 days’ written notice**.
• For fixed‑term leases, the landlord must provide a valid reason for early termination (e.g., breach of lease, property sale). | • Keep copies of all notices. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must serve a **30‑day notice** for non‑payment of rent or a **60‑day notice** for lease violations.
• If you fail to comply, the landlord can file an eviction action in district court. | • Respond promptly to notices; consider mediation or legal counsel. | | **Repair‑and‑Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to fix a major repair within a reasonable time, you may deduct the cost from rent (up to the amount of the repair). | • Keep receipts and provide written notice to the landlord before deducting. | | **Right to a Written Lease** | • While not required, a written lease protects both parties. | • Request a written lease if you’re signing a new agreement. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify which utilities you’re responsible for. | • Verify utility responsibilities before signing. | | **Subletting & Assignment** | • You may sublet or assign the lease only with the landlord’s written consent (unless the lease prohibits it). | • Obtain written permission and keep a copy. | | **Legal Remedies** | • Small‑claims court (up to $20,000) for disputes over rent, deposits, or repairs.
• Texas Attorney General’s Office for consumer protection issues. | • Gather documentation (photos, receipts, correspondence). | #### Quick Tips 1. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of the lease, receipts, emails, and a move‑in/move‑out inspection log. 2. **Know the Notice Periods** – 24 hrs for entry, 30 days for rent payment, 30/60 days for lease termination. 3. **Use Official Channels** – File complaints with TDHCA, TCHR, or HUD if you suspect unlawful behavior. 4. **Seek Legal Advice** – If you’re facing eviction or a dispute, consult a tenant‑rights attorney or a local legal aid organization. --- **Disclaimer:** This overview is for informational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. Laws can change, and specific circumstances may affect your rights. For personalized guidance, consult a licensed attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.
